quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When designing an ecological experiment for Environmental Science Requirement 1, how do biotic factors differ from abiotic factors, and what is the purpose of a control group?
quiz_item.question: When designing an ecological experiment for Environmental Science Requirement 1, how do biotic factors differ from abiotic factors, and what is the purpose of a control group?
options: A. Biotic factors are living components (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria) and abiotic factors are nonliving physical/chemical conditions (sunlight, temperature, soil pH, dissolved oxygen); the control group is kept at baseline conditions so you can isolate the effect of the single independent variable being tested.
B. Biotic factors are rocks and rainfall while abiotic factors are predators and pollinators; the control group has every variable changed at once.
C. Biotic and abiotic factors are identical synonyms for air pollution, and a scientific experiment never compares treated samples against untreated baselines.
D. Abiotic factors refer only to synthetic plastics, and the control group is discarded before recording any measurements.

requirements.lead_text: Air Pollution. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Air Pollution. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Learn what Particulate Matter (PM) is, how PM gets into the air, what the harmful effects of PM are, and what is being done to reduce PM in the air. Then, perform an experiment to test for particulates that contribute to air pollution. (b) Discuss how air pollution and transportation affect each other by giving at least three examples. Then, compare two modes of transportation (e. g., gasoline-powered vs. electric vehicles, gasoline-powered car vs. bicycle, etc.).
